title: Using headless AI playtests to balance my roguelite card game
author: Tommyruin
selftext:
I'm building **AITA: The Dark Domain**, a roguelite card game where a standard deck is both your attack system and your health pool. I wanted to share the AI-dev side because manual balance testing stopped scaling once the game had 100+ blessings, co-op rules, finale bosses, and lots of card-interaction edge cases.

https://preview.redd.it/2azssnp7u52h1.png?width=1920&format=png&auto=webp&s=88bc3e261fcb730318b39edaabef38fb026fe7d8

The useful part has been a headless simulator. It runs combat, campfire, progression, and finale logic without React or DOM dependencies, using the same reducer-style game rules as the browser client and multiplayer server. That means I can run thousands of simulated games without opening the UI, then compare whether solo, co-op, server authority, and the simulator resolve actions the same way.

The AI player is deliberately simple, with tunable weights for things like kill pressure, card conservation, hand value, yield tolerance, act pressure, and late-game risk. I then use an algorithm to evolve better weight sets through selection, crossover, and mutation. It allows for a consistent pressure-test player that catches broken balance and weird rule interactions before human testers have to find them.

One unexpectedly useful metric is a Blessing Power Index. Each starting blessing can be benchmarked against a baseline, so outliers show up quickly: blessings that are too strong, too weak, or only look fair because the bot does not understand a human-facing downside or strategy yet.

The biggest design lesson so far: AI blindspots expose fake downsides. If a curse is supposed to hurt the player but the headless player wins more often with it, the downside probably needs real mechanical teeth instead of just being visual friction or UI inconvenience.

The public solo beta is playable now: [https://aitatdd.com/play](https://aitatdd.com/play)

I'm aiming for Steam, iOS, and Android later, but right now the build is a web/PWA and that is how I mostly play and test it.

I also have a small closed beta code batch for people who specifically want to test the full beta/co-op side. That is not the main point of this post, but comment if that is useful and I can DM a code.

Curious how other people here are handling AI-assisted balance testing. Are you using bots as real QA tools, or mostly as content/dev assistants?

comments.author: Vivid-Snow-2089
comments.body:
Yeah I'm working on something like a text based twine-like aurora 4x deep simulation game. Right from the get go I knew I was going to leave all coding to the AI and just manage the design/mechanics and feel of the game and not care about anything else. One thing I knew I would need was a lot of testing so the AI can actually get feedback and make sure what it does is correct.

Since its browser based that is relatively simple now, and for play testing an agent will just spin up a few seperate browser sessions on different ports and play the game in parallel. Pretty fun watching codex and claude in a grid clicking through all the UI interfaces.

Funniest time was when the directive was 'earn 100,000 credits' and claude found a stable loop that would be super boring for a player... but really simple for him to make a script that just picked the same exact actions over and over again to get there super fast....

replies.author: Tommyruin
replies.body: I was thinking of trying to get codex to browser test the game, but it was extremely slow and I thought it would drain my usage! It's funny seeing how they quite quickly default to the stable loops that get results, especially when not clear to humans.

replies.author: Vivid-Snow-2089
replies.body:
Since my game is heavily text based I can provide a LLM native delta snapshot with every action. When not testing the UI there is also a LLM native control surface that's all token efficient so it doesn't have to screenshot every turn. It also uses a fast mini model that's dumb but basically instant as a sort of script to make thinks smoother for itself... the result is some modes are just super fast during testing.

I usually am using the UI testing though, because that catches a lot of issues.

And yeah, if you don't specify a specific objective or goal in the game, and give something generic like earn X amount of money... that's when you find the exploits, lol.
